about: Two courses fused, grouped by idea: Signals and systems 1 after Prechtl (2010), Vorlesungen über Signale und Systeme 1, TU Wien (continuous time), and Signals and systems 2 after Doblinger (2015), Zeitdiskrete Signale und Systeme, 3rd edition (discrete time). Each lab shows the continuous signal beside the discrete one where both exist. Laplace and z-transform, Bode diagrams, the state space and controllability are left to the Automation lab. Sections and page ranges are those of the two texts' tables of contents (read on 1 Nov 2026); each equation names its section, equation number and printed page, checked against the texts on 1 Nov 2026 (AUDIT.md). Where the texts write a quantity with their own symbol (Doblinger's θ, f_g, h_d, c_k; Prechtl's Q₁, k_i, R_xx) the lab does too; the signal letters x, y, h and the system operator S stay one vocabulary across both courses (Prechtl writes u, y, g and S[·], Doblinger T{·}). Practice answers are worked by hand or taken from the course's exercise collection, each naming its source; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

labs.title: Shifting and scaling time
labs.idea: Shift, reverse and scale the time axis: a signal only moves and stretches, a sequence scaled by M loses samples.
labs.law: y(t) = x(at − t0)    y[n] = x[Mn + n0]
labs.lawTex: y(t) = x(at - t_0) \qquad y[n] = x[Mn + n_0]
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), section 1.2, pp. 5–12; Doblinger (2015), section 2.2, pp. 15–18, and (8.26), p. 201

equations.note: scaled by a, shifted to start at t = t0/a
reversed in time
shift by a whole number of samples
keep every M-th sample (M a whole number)

practice.question: x[n] = 1 for n = 0 … 4 and 0 elsewhere. How many samples of y[n] = x[2n − 3] are not zero?
practice.solution: y[n] ≠ 0 where 0 ≤ 2n − 3 ≤ 4, so 1.5 ≤ n ≤ 3.5: n = 2 and n = 3. Two samples, x[1] and x[3]; x[0], x[2] and x[4] are lost.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 2.2

labs.title: Linearity and time invariance
labs.idea: Test a system: does the output of a sum equal the sum of the outputs, and does a delayed input give a delayed output?
labs.law: S{a x1 + b x2} = a S{x1} + b S{x2}    S{x(t − t0)} = y(t − t0)
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), section 1.4, pp. 18–23; Doblinger (2015), section 3.1, pp. 30–44

equations.eq: S{a x1 + b x2} = a S{x1} + b S{x2}
equations.note: linear: superposition holds (from rest)

equations.tex: y(t) = S\{x(t)\} \;\Rightarrow\; y(t - t_0) = S\{x(t - t_0)\}
equations.note: time-invariant

equations.tex: y[n] = S\{x[n]\} \;\Rightarrow\; y[n - n_0] = S\{x[n - n_0]\}
equations.note: shift-invariant sequence system

practice.question: An LTI system's step response is s(t) = (1 − e^(−t/τ)) V with τ = 1 s. The input is a pulse of height 1 from t = 0 to t = 1 s. What is the output at t = 2 s?
practice.solution: The pulse is a step minus a step delayed by 1 s. By linearity and time invariance y(t) = s(t) − s(t − 1 s), so y(2 s) = (1 − e^(−2)) − (1 − e^(−1)) = e^(−1) − e^(−2) = 0.2325 V. (Prechtl writes h(t) for the step response, (1.67), and g(t) for the impulse response.)
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 1.4, (1.51) and (1.55), pp. 22–24

labs.title: Convolution
labs.idea: Flip the impulse response, slide it, multiply and add up: the output of any LTI system, integral or sum.
labs.law: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ    y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n − k]
labs.lawTex: y(t) = \int x(\tau)\, h(t - \tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \qquad y[n] = \sum_k x[k]\, h[n - k]
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), section 1.5, pp. 24–28; Doblinger (2015), section 3.1, pp. 30–44

equations.eq: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ = (x ∗ h)(t)
equations.note: convolution integral
commutative
convolution sum
for finite sequences; follows from (3.7), counted by hand

practice.question: A pulse of height 1 and length 1 s enters a system with h(t) = e^(−t/τ) for t ≥ 0, τ = 0.5 s. What is y(t) at t = 1 s?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 1.5, (1.62), p. 27

labs.title: Random signals and correlation
labs.idea: White noise forgets at once; a low-pass gives it memory. Cross-correlation finds an echo buried in noise.
labs.law: r_xx[k] = E[x[n] x[n + k]]    σy² = σx² (1 − a)/(1 + a)
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), sections 1.3 and 4.6, pp. 13–17, 101–106; the discrete forms are the lab's own (Doblinger (2015) has no section on random signals)

equations.note: autocorrelation of a stationary process

equations.eq: r_xy(τ) = lim (1/T) ∫ x(t) y(t + τ) dt
equations.note: cross-correlation of jointly ergodic signals
noise through an LTI system: power spectra (Prechtl writes G for H)
the lab's low-pass

equations.eq: σy² = σx² (1 − a)/(1 + a), r_yy[k]/r_yy[0] = a^|k|
equations.note: its output for white input

practice.question: White noise of variance 1 passes through y[n] = 0.9 y[n − 1] + 0.1 x[n]. What is the output's variance?
practice.source: Worked by hand; the discrete counterpart of Prechtl (2010), section 4.6, (4.32) and (4.34), pp. 103–104

labs.title: Fourier series
labs.idea: A periodic signal is a sum of harmonics; at a jump, the partial sums always overshoot. A periodic sequence needs only N.
labs.law: x(t) = Σ c_k e^(j2πkt/T)    x[n] = Σ_{k=0}^{N−1} c_k e^(j2πkn/N)
labs.lawTex: x(t) = \sum_k c_k\, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}2\pi k t/T} \qquad x[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k\, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}2\pi k n/N}
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), chapter 5, pp. 108–121; Doblinger (2015), section 2.3, pp. 19–28

equations.eq: x(t) = Σₖ c_k e^(j2πkt/T),  c_k = (1/T) ∫_T x(t) e^(−j2πkt/T) dt
equations.tex: x(t) = \sum_k c_k\, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}2\pi k t/T}, \qquad c_k = \frac{1}{T} \int_T x(t)\, \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j}2\pi k t/T}\,\mathrm{d}t
equations.note: Fourier series (Prechtl writes C_k, T₁)
c_k = 2/(jπk) for odd k, so the sine amplitude is 4/(πk)

equations.tex: x[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k\, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}2\pi k n/N}, \qquad c_k = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j}2\pi k n/N}
equations.note: discrete Fourier series, period N; c_k = X[k]/N

equations.eq: max of partial sum → 1 + 0.179 for a jump from −1 to 1
equations.tex: \text{max of partial sum} \to 1 + 0.179 \quad \text{for a jump from } {-1} \text{ to } 1
equations.note: Gibbs overshoot, about 9 % of the jump (Prechtl, p. 113); the value (2/π) Si(π) = 1.179 is by definition

practice.question: A square wave jumps between −1 and +1. What is the amplitude of its third harmonic?
practice.solution: c_k = 2/(jπk) for odd k (Prechtl (5.17)), and c_k e^(jkτ) + c_−k e^(−jkτ) = j2c_k sin(kτ) (5.43), so b_k = 4/(πk) and b_3 = 4/(3π) = 0.424.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 5.1, (5.17), p. 113, and (5.43), p. 118

labs.title: Fourier transform
labs.idea: Shorter in time is wider in frequency. A sequence has the same spectrum near zero, but repeated every sampling rate.
labs.law: X(f) = ∫ x(t) e^(−j2πft) dt    X(e^jθ) = Σ x[n] e^(−jθn)
labs.lawTex: X(f) = \int x(t)\, \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j}2\pi f t}\,\mathrm{d}t \qquad X(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}\theta}) = \sum_n x[n]\, \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j}\theta n}
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), sections 3.1–3.3, pp. 65–79; Doblinger (2015), chapter 4 and section 4.1, pp. 59–73

equations.note: Fourier transform over f (Prechtl writes U(jf))
pulse and its spectrum; sinc x = sin(πx)/(πx), Prechtl's rect(τ) ↔ si(ω/2) with si x = sin x / x
time scaling (Prechtl: Zeitdehnung), written over f
Fourier transform of a sequence (DTFT)

practice.question: A pulse lasts 1 ms. At what frequency is its spectrum first zero?
practice.solution: X(f) = T sinc(fT) is zero where fT = 1, at f = 1/T = 1 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 3.1, (3.22), p. 71: si(ω/2) first vanishes at ω = 2π, that is f = 1/T

labs.title: Harmonics and power
labs.idea: Harmonics in the current add RMS current and apparent power but no active power: they are distortion power.
labs.law: S² = P² + Q₁² + D²    k_i = √(Σ_{k>1} |I_k|²) / I

equations.note: RMS of a current with harmonics, each |I_k| an RMS value

equations.eq: P = U |I_1| cos φ_1,  Q₁ = U |I_1| sin φ_1
equations.note: with a sine voltage, only the fundamental carries P and the fundamental reactive power Q₁

equations.tex: S = U I, \qquad D = U \sqrt{|I_2|^2 + |I_3|^2 + \cdots} = k_i\, S
equations.note: apparent and distortion power; Prechtl's reactive power Q obeys Q² = Q₁² + D²
power factor; g_i = |I_1|/I is the fundamental content (6.12)

practice.question: A 230 V sine voltage drives a current of 10 A (fundamental, in phase), 3 A at the third and 2 A at the fifth harmonic, all RMS. What is the RMS current?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 6.2, (6.10), p. 123

practice.question: For the same current, what is the distortion power D?
practice.solution: D = U √(|I_3|² + |I_5|²) = 230 × √13 VA = 829 VA. Check: P = 2300 W, Q₁ = 0, S = 230 × 10.63 VA = 2445 VA, and √(S² − P²) gives the same 829 VA.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 6.3, (6.28), p. 127

labs.title: DFT, windows and the FFT
labs.idea: N samples give N lines that sample the spectrum; a sine between lines leaks, a window tames it, the FFT gets there fast.
labs.law: X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N)    Δf = fs/N
labs.lecture: Doblinger (2015), chapter 7 and sections 7.1, 7.2, 7.4 and 7.6, pp. 165–175, 180, 186–190

equations.note: DFT
the DFT samples the transform on the unit circle
line spacing: θ = 2πk/N with θ = 2πf/fs (4.53)
radix-2 FFT, one complex product each; Doblinger counts N log₂ N operations against N² (p. 189)

practice.question: A DFT of N = 1024 samples is taken at fs = 8 kHz. How far apart are its lines?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), (7.27), p. 175, and (4.53), p. 76

labs.title: Sampling and aliasing
labs.idea: Sample fast enough and sincs rebuild the signal exactly; too slowly, and the samples fit a slower sine instead.
labs.law: x(t) = Σ x[n] sinc((t − nT)/T)    fs > 2 f_g

equations.note: ideal sampling, fs = 1/T
the spectrum repeats every fs
sampling theorem, for a signal band-limited to f_g
ideal reconstruction; Doblinger writes sin(ω_g(t − nT))/(ω_g(t − nT)) with ω_g = π/T
where a sine folds to

practice.question: A 7 kHz sine is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear?
practice.solution: 7 kHz is above fs/2 = 5 kHz; it folds to |7 − 10| kHz = 3 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 4.2, (4.52)–(4.54), pp. 76–77

practice.question: Samples x[0] = 1 and all others 0 are rebuilt ideally. What is x(t) halfway between the first two samples?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 4.2, (4.61), p. 78

labs.title: Digital filters
labs.idea: An IIR filter from an analogue Butterworth by the bilinear transform, or an FIR filter from a windowed sinc.
labs.law: s = 2fs (z − 1)/(z + 1)    ωa = 2fs tan(π fc / fs)    h[n] = 2Fc sinc(2Fc (n − (N−1)/2)) w[n]
labs.lawTex: s = 2 f_\mathrm{s}\, \frac{z - 1}{z + 1} \qquad \omega_\mathrm{a} = 2 f_\mathrm{s} \tan\frac{\pi f_\mathrm{c}}{f_\mathrm{s}} \qquad h[n] = 2F_\mathrm{c} \operatorname{sinc}\!\Big(2F_\mathrm{c}\Big(n - \frac{N - 1}{2}\Big)\Big)\, w[n]

equations.note: Butterworth prototype; Doblinger writes it normalised to the 3 dB frequency, ω_a = 1
bilinear transform, 2/T with T = 1/fs
pre-warping: (6.58), ω = (2/T) tan(θ/2), at θ_c = 2π fc/fs
window method; h_d the ideal filter, for a low-pass (6.2) delayed by n0 = (N − 1)/2 (6.38, N odd)

equations.eq: w[n] = a0 − a1 cos(2πn/(N−1)) + a2 cos(4πn/(N−1))
equations.tex: w[n] = a_0 - a_1 \cos\frac{2\pi n}{N - 1} + a_2 \cos\frac{4\pi n}{N - 1}

practice.question: A digital low-pass at fs = 8 kHz should cut off at 1 kHz by the bilinear transform. To what frequency is the analogue prototype pre-warped?
practice.solution: ωa = 2fs tan(π fc/fs) = 16000 tan(π/8) s⁻¹ = 6627 s⁻¹, so fa = ωa/2π = 1055 Hz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 6.3.2, (6.58), p. 149

practice.question: A first-order digital low-pass with its 3 dB cut-off at fg = fs/10 is made from Ha(s) = 1/(1 + s) by the bilinear transform. Where on the real axis of the z-plane is its pole?
practice.source: Doblinger et al. (2016), Signale und Systeme 2, Beispielsammlung, Aufgabe 5.4 a, p. 22, Lösung p. 85

practice.question: An ideal low-pass with normalised cut-off Fc = 0.125 has h[n] = 2Fc sinc(2Fc n). What is h[2]?
practice.solution: h[2] = 0.25 sinc(0.5) = 0.25 × 2/π = 0.159. In Doblinger's form, h[n] = sin(θg n)/(πn) with θg = 2πFc = π/4: sin(π/2)/(2π) = 0.159.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 6.1, (6.2), p. 120

labs.title: Changing the sampling rate
labs.idea: Keep every M-th sample and what lay above fs/(2M) folds into the band; filter first. Insert zeros, filter after.

equations.note: downsampling (Doblinger: y[n] = w[nM], after the filter)
its spectrum: stretched and folded
upsampling: L − 1 zeros between samples
its spectrum: images

practice.question: A 48 kHz signal is to be downsampled by M = 4. Up to what frequency may the anti-aliasing filter pass?
practice.solution: The new rate is 12 kHz, so the band must end at fs/(2M) = 6 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 8.2, (8.31), p. 202: the filter passes |θ| < π/M, that is f < fs/(2M)
